title.en: Sum of n terms of a G.P.

heading.en: The chessboard and the grains of rice

hook.en: One grain on the first square, two on the next, four on the next. The 64 squares together need 2⁶⁴ − 1 grains, far more rice than the world grows in centuries.
hook.kn: ಮೊದಲ ಚೌಕದಲ್ಲಿ ಒಂದು ಕಾಳು, ಮುಂದಿನದರಲ್ಲಿ ಎರಡು, ನಂತರ ನಾಲ್ಕು. 64 ಚೌಕಗಳಿಗೆ ಒಟ್ಟು 2⁶⁴ − 1 ಕಾಳುಗಳು ಬೇಕು, ಜಗತ್ತು ಶತಮಾನಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಬೆಳೆಯುವುದಕ್ಕಿಂತ ಹೆಚ್ಚು.

objectives.en: Derive and use Sₙ for a G.P.
Use the sum to infinity when |r| < 1

narration.en: One grain on the first square, two on the next, four on the next. The 64 squares together need 2⁶⁴ − 1 grains, far more rice than the world grows in centuries.
narration.kn: ಮೊದಲ ಚೌಕದಲ್ಲಿ ಒಂದು ಕಾಳು, ಮುಂದಿನದರಲ್ಲಿ ಎರಡು, ನಂತರ ನಾಲ್ಕು. 64 ಚೌಕಗಳಿಗೆ ಒಟ್ಟು 2⁶⁴ − 1 ಕಾಳುಗಳು ಬೇಕು, ಜಗತ್ತು ಶತಮಾನಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಬೆಳೆಯುವುದಕ್ಕಿಂತ ಹೆಚ್ಚು.

body.en: Write $S_n = a + ar + \dots + ar^{n-1}$, multiply by $r$ and subtract: $(1 - r)S_n = a(1 - r^n)$. So for $r \neq 1$, $S_n = \frac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r} = \frac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$, and for $r = 1$, $S_n = na$.
body.kn: Sₙ ಅನ್ನು r ನಿಂದ ಗುಣಿಸಿ ಕಳೆಯುವುದರಿಂದ ಸೂತ್ರ ಸಿಗುತ್ತದೆ: r ≠ 1 ಆದಾಗ Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); r = 1 ಆದಾಗ Sₙ = na.

narration.en: Multiply the sum by r and subtract; almost every term cancels. That gives S n equals a times r to the n minus one, over r minus one.
narration.kn: Sₙ ಅನ್ನು r ನಿಂದ ಗುಣಿಸಿ ಕಳೆಯುವುದರಿಂದ ಸೂತ್ರ ಸಿಗುತ್ತದೆ: r ≠ 1 ಆದಾಗ Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); r = 1 ಆದಾಗ Sₙ = na.

narration.en: Write the sum, then multiply every term by r. The two lines share almost all their terms.

say.en: Write the sum, then multiply every term by r. The two lines share almost all their terms.
Subtract: everything cancels except a r to the n and a. Divide by r minus 1.
Now cut a square in half, then the leftover in half, again and again. The pieces one half, one quarter, one eighth and so on fill the whole square.
When r is between minus 1 and 1, r to the n goes to zero, so the sum to infinity is a over 1 minus r. That turns 0.333 recurring into one third.

body.en: When $|r| < 1$, $r^n \to 0$ as $n$ grows, so $S_n$ approaches $S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 - r}$. For example, $1 + \frac12 + \frac14 + \dots = 2$. This result is used often in KCET and JEE problems.
body.kn: |r| < 1 ಆದಾಗ rⁿ ಶೂನ್ಯದತ್ತ ಸಾಗುತ್ತದೆ; ಆಗ ಅನಂತ ಪದಗಳ ಮೊತ್ತ a/(1 − r).

narration.en: If the common ratio lies between minus one and one, the terms shrink to zero and the sum settles at a over one minus r.
narration.kn: |r| < 1 ಆದಾಗ rⁿ ಶೂನ್ಯದತ್ತ ಸಾಗುತ್ತದೆ; ಆಗ ಅನಂತ ಪದಗಳ ಮೊತ್ತ a/(1 − r).

caption.en: The yellow curve is Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r); the green line is S∞ = a/(1 − r). Change a, r and n and watch the gap close.

narration.en: The yellow curve is Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r); the green line is S∞ = a/(1 − r). Change a, r and n and watch the gap close. With a = 1, r = 0.5, how many terms make Sₙ within 0.01 of 2?

tryThis.en: With a = 1, r = 0.5, how many terms make Sₙ within 0.01 of 2?
Push r up to 0.95: the limit is far away and the sums crawl towards it.
Set a = 0.9 and r = 0.1: the sum to infinity is 0.999… = 1.

problem.en: Find the sum of the first 8 terms of the G.P. 3, 6, 12, …

narration.en: Let us solve this together. Find the sum of the first 8 terms of the G.P. 3, 6, 12, …

problem.en: How many terms of the G.P. 3, 3/2, 3/4, … are needed to give the sum 3069/512?

narration.en: Let us solve this together. How many terms of the G.P. 3, 3/2, 3/4, … are needed to give the sum 3069/512?

body.en: A two-digit block repeating for ever is that block over 99: 0.454545… = 45/99 = 5/11. One repeating digit goes over 9: 0.777… = 7/9.

narration.en: Recurring decimals are infinite G.P.s. A two-digit block repeating for ever is that block over 99: 0.454545… = 45/99 = 5/11. One repeating digit goes over 9: 0.777… = 7/9.
Class quiz. Discuss, raise hands, and the monitor taps the class answer.
narration.kn: ತರಗತಿ ರಸಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ. ಚರ್ಚಿಸಿ, ಕೈ ಎತ್ತಿ, ಮಾನಿಟರ್ ತರಗತಿಯ ಉತ್ತರವನ್ನು ಒತ್ತಲಿ.

narration.en: Now two exam-pattern questions of the kind asked in KCET, COMEDK and JEE. Try them before we discuss.

Now 3 CBSE board-pattern questions: assertion–reason and case-based. For assertion–reason, judge A and R separately before asking whether R explains A. For the case, read the situation and apply today's idea step by step.

points.en: Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1; Sₙ = na for r = 1.
points.kn: r ≠ 1 ಆದಾಗ Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); r = 1 ಆದಾಗ Sₙ = na.

points.en: For |r| < 1 the infinite sum is a/(1 − r).
Recurring decimals can be written as fractions using a G.P.
points.kn: ಆವರ್ತ ದಶಮಾಂಶಗಳನ್ನು ಗುಣೋತ್ತರ ಶ್ರೇಢಿ ಬಳಸಿ ಭಿನ್ನರಾಶಿಯಾಗಿ ಬರೆಯಬಹುದು.

homework.en: Find the sum of the first 10 terms of 0.15, 0.015, 0.0015, …

narration.en: Recap. Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1; Sₙ = na for r = 1. For |r| < 1 the infinite sum is a/(1 − r). Recurring decimals can be written as fractions using a G.P.
narration.kn: ಪುನರಾವರ್ತನೆ. r ≠ 1 ಆದಾಗ Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); r = 1 ಆದಾಗ Sₙ = na. |r| < 1 ಆದಾಗ ಅನಂತ ಮೊತ್ತ a/(1 − r). ಆವರ್ತ ದಶಮಾಂಶಗಳನ್ನು ಗುಣೋತ್ತರ ಶ್ರೇಢಿ ಬಳಸಿ ಭಿನ್ನರಾಶಿಯಾಗಿ ಬರೆಯಬಹುದು.
